blocks: Electro-Active Polymer Research for LIMS Applications
The information presented in this paper is the result of a quarter of research for the Laboratory for Intelligent Mechanical Systems (LIMS) in the field of Electro-active Polymers (EAPs).

LIMS is a research laboratory of the Mechanical Engineering Department of Northwestern University in Illinois that concerns itself with robotics and other applications that use the integration of electromechanical systems and computer controls to achieve various goals. Recently, the Office of Naval Research has approached this laboratory with the ambitious project of investigating fish propulsion systems. Though many watercraft employ fish-inspired stream-lined hull geometries and smoothed surfaces, boat builders have avoided the imitation of tail fins because of the tail's large movements. It has been determined, however, that specialized fish driven by their pectoral fins as well as those who utilize a “ribbon fin” on their underbelly for propulsion have the potential to be mechanically imitated. The end goal of this endeavor would be to utilize the efficiencies obtained through millions of years of evolution to improve on current propeller driven remotely operated vehicles (ROV) and submersibles.

Another advantage that these fish have is exceptional maneuverability. The ribbon fin of the knife fish and pectoral fins of the wrasse are of interest. The wrasse's fins allow flight-like motion through the water as the pectoral fins are manipulated to create lift. The knife fish's “ribbon” allows for complete reversal of direction literally on a dime, even at top speed. If proven effective as intelligent mechanical systems, fish inspired propulsion methods could even make their way to large-scale war submarines in the future.

Current technologies dictate that the standard in actuating any fin apparatus that might be built is electromagnetic motors. These motors can be electrically controlled and therefore mesh very well with software control systems. Unfortunately, these motors are only standard as linear or angular actuators. Consequently, any motions that do not have a circular or linear path will require sometimes-complicated apparatuses on top of the motors themselves. Additionally, motors are very

difficult to scale down to the centimeter range. In fish fins, the wrasse's pectoral fin is driven by a stiff leading edge. With some work, this fin could be imitated by a combination of motors and mechanisms. The ribbon fin, however, has proven more difficult to imitate with motors, (as seen by Professor Maciver's mechanical fin in Figure 1). Although functional for researching fluid forces generated by movement in water, the mechanism would not be ideal in a fully emerged submersible-like application due to its large size and weight.

In light of the end goal of creating a large-scale In light of the end goal of creating a large-scale mechanical pectoral or ribbon fin, LIMS has sought to investigate the emerging field of Electro-active polymers (EAPs) as actuators. EAPs are essentially polymers that have been manipulated in such a way that they transform electrical input (in this case voltage) into mechanical output (displacement). Due to the discovery of particular plastics and the novel use of compliant electrodes, researchers have demonstrated fast response times (<1ms), high efficiencies (80-90%), high area actuation strain (215%), and energy densities up to .15 J/g.² These claims along with the light weight of polymers have made EAPs very promising as actuators for eventual fin systems. EAPs come in two varieties; ionic and electronic.

Ionic EAPs use mechanisms of electro-chemistry, namely the movement of charged ions in the molecules of advanced materials. These materials include ionomeric polymer-metal composites, conductive polymers and even carbon nanotubes.³ Conventional batteries may be used with these EAPs, as voltages as low as 1V will activate movement.
